docs.title: FOREST
docs.text:
A video-first debate app. Someone posts a short video opinion, others answer with videos of their own, and an AI marks each reply as FOR, AGAINST or UNRESOLVED. A debate becomes a tree you can follow from the first opinion to the last reply.

Author(s): Sahibnoor Singh, Yaksh, Ridhima, Jasmine Tiwana (Group 1)

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
Debate tree Video Home Discover Question of the day Debate room Profile Create

Screenshots are from the Android app running on demo data. The accounts shown are automated demo accounts and are labelled BOT wherever they appear.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
1. Someone records a short video giving an opinion. That is the root of a debate.
  2. Anyone can reply with a video of their own.
  3. The audio is transcribed by an AI and each reply is placed against what it answers: FOR, AGAINST or UNRESOLVED. The AI says which side a reply is on. It does not decide who is right.
  4. The claims in a video are given a credibility score.
  5. Anyone can open the tree and go straight to the opposing side.

docs.title: Design and analysis models
docs.text: These are the models of the implemented FOREST system. Each one is explained in the final report (PDF, Word).

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: The User can both watch and create. The Moderator reviews reports. The Gemini API and the Email service are outside systems that take part.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Clients talk only to the server through Caddy, which handles HTTPS. The server is one process with a SQLite database and an upload folder, and it calls the Gemini API and an email provider.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text: Measured on the cloud machine with 2 000 users, 30 395 posts and 120 000 likes. Median and 95th percentile response times in milliseconds.

docs.title: 1. Project Overview
docs.text: Our project development is divided into four main phases. We start with a basic website and AI testing, and eventually build a full mobile app that real students can use. We make sure each phase is fully working before moving to the next one.

docs.title: 2. Milestone 1: Core Website and AI Testing
docs.text:
Status: Completed Target Date: September 18, 2026

In this phase, we focused on getting the core technology to work. * We designed the main database and backend system. * We gathered a small dataset of 20 political videos to test our idea manually. * We connected the Gemini API so it can read video audio and decide if a video is FOR or AGAINST a topic. * We launched a basic testing website where users can upload a transcript and see the graph build live.

docs.title: 3. Milestone 2: Mobile App and Better Graphs
docs.text:
Status: Mostly done, in internal testing Target Date: November 25, 2026

Now that the website works, we need to make it accessible for normal users on their phones. * We built a mobile application using Flutter. Users sign up with an e-mailed code or Google, record videos from their camera, and reply to each other with video. * The debate tree shows an opinion and all of its replies on one screen, coloured FOR or AGAINST, with a credibility score on each. * We added a question of the day, a list of opinions still waiting for a first reply, and debate rooms where a society or class argues one motion. * Automated demo accounts are always labelled BOT in the app. * Still to do: a community vote for replies the AI cannot place, for example sarcasm.

docs.title: 4. Milestone 3: Beta Launch
docs.text:
Status: Planned Target Date: January 30, 2027

This is our testing phase where we share the app with real people to see if it actually stops echo chambers. * We will invite about 100 university students to download the app and post debate videos. * We will track how people use the app to make sure it shows them different opinions, not just the ones they agree with. * We will add an automatic safety filter to block bad language or inappropriate videos.

docs.title: 5. Milestone 4: Final Presentation
docs.text:
Status: In progress

The final presentation of the project to the evaluation panel. * Present the working Flutter app: video feed, debate tree, question of the day and debate rooms. * Present the AI pipeline that places each reply as FOR, AGAINST or UNRESOLVED. * Submit the report and the team journals.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Sahibnoor Singh's Journal
docs.text:
I am the team leader. I worked on the main server connection and the database logic. In the first few weeks, I figured out how to connect our project to the Gemini API so we can process transcripts easily. I also set up the graph database so we can store opinions properly without losing data.

I make sure the team stays on track and I combine everyone's code into the main project at the end of the week.

Below is a dated log of what I actually did, taken from our commit history.

docs.title: August 2026: the first website prototype
docs.text:
11 to 19 August. I started the repository and built the first version of the FOREST website: an admin dashboard where content can be added, edited and deleted, a custom favicon, and a roadmap page showing the ten phases of the project. The part that took longest was the presentations page. Our plan was to show slide decks inside the site, so I tried an Office embed, then Google's viewer, then a browser PowerPoint renderer, and found each one either looked wrong or showed someone else's branding. I settled on converting each deck to PDF on the server and showing it with pdf.js, then fixed the layout so the controls never cover the slides. I also restricted the viewer to logged-in admins. I marked Prototype 1.0 complete on 19 August.

25 August. I added the debate graph screen, moved the graph pipeline onto its own testing page, set up a Neo4j Aura graph database, and added a Spring Boot backend to the repository for deployment. This is the graph database mentioned above. It holds the debate tree: which video is a reply to which, and on which side.

docs.title: September 2026: AI pipeline, proposal and deployment
docs.text:
13 to 15 September. This was our busiest stretch as a team. - Merged the Gemini Flash transcription work through three pull requests, and fixed a Spring Boot address setting that had been overwritten when branches were combined. - Wrote the project Gantt chart, and added the proposal and the feasibility report. - Set up automatic deployment with GitHub Actions to our Oracle cloud server, so a push to main updates the live site. - Built the "AI Lab" page: a live view of the pipeline as it runs, with a log panel and a transcript viewer, and a layout the user can resize. - Gemini's free limits kept running out, so I made the backend try several Gemini models in order and fall back to a second API key when one is exhausted. - Protected our data: removed the database and uploaded media from version control, added two rolling snapshots of the SQLite database with automatic recovery, and fixed a bug where re-uploading could clash on an existing ID. - Fixed smaller problems: the admin publish button failing silently because of a missing database column, and expired logins leaving the page stuck.

22 September. First commits of the Flutter mobile app. From here the project moves from a website to an Android app.

docs.title: October 2026: the mobile app
docs.text:
10 to 15 October. I built the app's Home screen against our API contract: the feed of opinion cards, replying by recording, choosing from the gallery or typing, a thread view with nested replies, likes, and report and block from a menu. I also built the colour theme (light and dark), a video cache and player pool so scrolling stays smooth, and handling for when the server is busy. On 12 October I merged Yaksh's Discover reels page into the app. By 13 October there was login and sign-up, and I added seed scripts and a shared snapshot so that any teammate sees the same demo data. On 14 October I added subtitles: Gemini returns timed caption lines with the transcript, the language is detected, English captions are made, and the viewer has a language picker (Off, Original, English, Hindi, Punjabi and others).

17 October. The post editor, on both the server and the app. A person can make a video, photo slideshow or text post, trim and crop, add music from the phone, put text over the picture, and choose a colour look. The server renders the result with FFmpeg. I also made text in Hindi and Punjabi draw correctly.

19 to 22 October. A large week of features: - Discover: a grid ranked for each person, search over posts and accounts, sending a video to a friend, and a feed that learns a little from what friends send. - Messages inbox, report with a reason, block, and a list of blocked accounts. - Sign-up by an e-mailed code, instead of paid SMS, and Continue with Google, with the server checking Google's token itself. - Onboarding for new users, and a redesigned login and sign-up. - The question of the day, a "waiting for an answer" strip for opinions nobody has replied to, debate rooms where a society argues one motion, and invite codes. - Product events and a private numbers page for the team.

27 October. Merged Yaksh's profile page into the main app (pull request 7) and joined it with the Account tab.

docs.title: November 2026: polish, review and hosting
docs.text:
• A polish pass on the video screen and Home, a notifications list with a badge, and clearer wording when something fails, so users never see a raw error.
  • Wrote the files to host the server on a cloud machine: a Docker setup with automatic HTTPS, nightly backups, an update script, a settings check, and a cost estimate. These are written and checked but not yet run on a real machine.
  • Reviewed the new server code for bugs and fixed ten of them: a limit on rooms that counted finished rooms, wrong dates for a different time zone, suspended accounts still visible, blocked people appearing in lists, counts that did not match what was shown, and a slow profile page. Each fix has its own automated test.
  • The project now has about 365 automated tests on the server and about 540 in the app, and they all pass.

docs.title: Working with the team
docs.text: I keep the main branch up to date and merge each person's branch into it, and when a merge touched someone else's files I wrote them a short note on what changed. Yaksh's Discover and profile work and Ridhima's audio clean-up script both went in through this process. The next step on my side is hosting the server so the team can test the app on real phones.

docs.title: Jasmine's Journal
docs.text:
I am in charge of collecting the data to test our project. I gathered a bunch of Instagram reel links about different debate topics, like student protests. I saved them in a document so the other team members can download them and run them through our code.

I also help test the final website by uploading the transcripts and making sure the graph connects the arguments properly.

docs.title: Yaksh's Journal
docs.text:
I am responsible for the website layout and how the graph looks on the screen. I designed the drag and drop boxes so users can easily upload their transcripts. I also worked on the script that takes the audio file and sends it to the server so we can get the text back.

We had some trouble with the graph zooming out too far, so I added a button to center the screen properly.

docs.title: Ridhima's Journal
docs.text:
I worked on the Python side of our project. My main job was to figure out how to separate background music from the person speaking in the video. I built a script that uses the Demucs tool to clean the audio before we send it to the AI.

If we don't clean the audio, the AI gets confused by the music, so my script is very important for making the text accurate.
